When Does Trajectory-Level Supervision Permit Efficient Offline Reinforcement Learning?

Xuanfei Ren University of Wisconsin-Madison Madison, WI xuanfeiren@cs.wisc.edu   Tengyang Xie University of Wisconsin-Madison Madison, WI tx@cs.wisc.edu ††thanks: Corresponding author.
Abstract

Offline reinforcement learning is typically analyzed under process-level reward supervision, yet many sequential decision datasets record only trajectory-level outcomes. We develop a statistical theory for offline policy optimization from such outcome-level supervision. We first study the canonical setting where the target remains the expected cumulative reward, but each offline trajectory provides only a scalar label whose conditional mean is the cumulative return. We propose OPAC, a pessimistic actor-critic algorithm that learns a latent reward model and optimizes a policy from trajectory-level labels. We prove a high-probability guarantee of order O~​(H2​Cs​a​(π⋆)/n)\widetilde{O}(H^{2}\sqrt{C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})/n}) and a matching lower bound, characterizing the sharp statistical cost of replacing process-level rewards with one trajectory-level label. We then extend the principle to preference-based feedback, preserving the leading horizon and concentrability dependence up to preference-model constants. Finally, we study generalized outcome-based offline RL, where both the supervision and the objective are trajectory-level quantities induced by a nonlinear aggregation of latent per-step rewards. This problem is not learnable in general: for all-success objectives, any offline learner may require Ω⁡(2H)\Omega(2^{H}) trajectories even with deterministic transitions and constant concentrability. We then identify a tractable regime through two structural coefficients, κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma) and χμ​(σ)\chi_{\mu}(\sigma), capturing information loss in outcome aggregation and generalized Bellman updates, under which generalized OPAC achieves polynomial sample complexity. Together, our results delineate when outcome-level supervision enables sample-efficient offline control and when missing process-level rewards create fundamental statistical barriers.

1 Introduction

Offline reinforcement learning asks whether a good policy can be learned from a fixed dataset of past interactions (Lange et al., 2012; Levine et al., 2020; Jiang and Xie, 2025), with a rich line of empirical algorithms developed in deep RL (Fujimoto et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2020; Fujimoto and Gu, 2021; Kostrikov et al., 2021, e.g.,). Most theory assumes that each trajectory is annotated with process-level rewards (Agarwal et al., 2022; Foster and Rakhlin, 2023): after every action, the learner observes the reward assigned to that state-action pair. This assumption gives direct access to Bellman targets, but it is often stronger than the supervision available in long-horizon applications. A dataset may record only whether a task eventually succeeded (Andrychowicz et al., 2017; Lightman et al., 2023), what final score was achieved, whether a proof was accepted (Uesato et al., 2022), whether a patient recovered (Komorowski et al., 2018; Gottesman et al., 2019), or which of two completed trajectories a human preferred (Christiano et al., 2017). The feedback is trajectory-level, while the decisions remain sequential (Jia et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025).

This paper develops a statistical theory for offline policy optimization from outcome-level supervision. The central question is not only whether such supervision is sufficient, but also where the statistical difficulty comes from: distribution shift in offline control (Xie et al., 2021a; Cheng et al., 2022; Jiang and Xie, 2025), recovering latent per-step rewards from aggregated labels (Jia et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025), or the trajectory-level objective itself (Zhang et al., 2020). We show that these sources of difficulty lead to qualitatively different regimes.

We begin with the regime closest to classical offline RL. The target objective is the usual expected cumulative reward J⁡(π)=𝔼τ∼π​[∑h=1Hr⋆​(sh,ah)]J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi}\left[\sum_{h=1}^{H}r^{\star}(s_{h},a_{h})\right], but the offline data do not reveal the per-step rewards. Instead, each sampled trajectory is labeled by a scalar outcome whose conditional mean is the cumulative return. Thus the objective is unchanged and only the observation model is weakened. This isolates a basic statistical question:

What is the cost of replacing HH local reward observations by one trajectory-level label?

We answer this question with matching upper and lower bounds, up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm, OPAC, is a pessimistic actor-critic method that jointly learns a latent per-step reward and a value function. The reward model is fit by trajectory-level regression, the critic is constrained through a plug-in Bellman error, and the policy update uses pessimism to account for distribution shift in the offline data (Xie et al., 2021a). Under standard realizability and completeness assumptions, for bounded per-step rewards and bounded trajectory outcomes, the output policy satisfies J⁡(π⋆)−J⁡(π¯)=O~​(H2​Cs​a​(π⋆)/n)J(\pi^{\star})-J(\bar{\pi})=\widetilde{O}\left(H^{2}\sqrt{{C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})}/{n}}\right), or equivalently needs O~​(H4​Cs​a​(π⋆)/ε2)\widetilde{O}(H^{4}C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})/\varepsilon^{2}) trajectories for ε\varepsilon-optimality (Theorem 1). We also prove an Ω⁡(H4/ε2)\Omega(H^{4}/\varepsilon^{2}) trajectory lower bound at constant state-action concentrability (Theorem 2). The hard instance has deterministic transitions and only two actions, so the additional factor relative to process-level reward supervision is not caused by exploration or transition estimation; it comes from compressing reward information into a single scalar outcome.

We then consider a weaker but practically important form of trajectory-level feedback: pairwise preferences. The learner observes which of two trajectories is preferred, generated by a Bradley–Terry–Luce model (Bradley and Terry, 1952; Christiano et al., 2017), while the optimization target remains the same cumulative return. The same algorithmic template applies after replacing squared trajectory-return regression with logistic preference regression. The resulting guarantee preserves the leading H2​Cs​a​(π⋆)/nH^{2}\sqrt{C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})/n} dependence, up to preference model constants (Theorem 3). Thus, for the standard cumulative-reward objective, calibrated scalar outcomes are not essential: sufficiently informative comparisons can support the same pessimistic offline-control mechanism.

The classical cumulative reward, however, is only one way trajectory-level feedback can arise. In many problems, the observed outcome is not merely a noisy proxy for cumulative reward, but the performance criterion itself. This motivates a generalized RL formulation in which the environment still admits latent per-step reward primitives, while policies are evaluated through a known trajectory-level aggregation rule. Concretely, for any candidate reward process r=(r1,…,rH)r=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{H}), define R⁡(τ,r)=σ⁡(r1​(s1,a1),…,rH​(sH,aH))R(\tau;r)=\sigma(r_{1}(s_{1},a_{1}),\ldots,r_{H}(s_{H},a_{H})), where σ:ℝH→[0,Vmax]\sigma:\mathbb{R}^{H}\to[0,V_{\max}] is known and may be nonlinear. The learning objective is

J⁡(π)=𝔼τ∼π​[σ⁡(r1⋆​(s1,a1),…,rH⋆​(sH,aH))].\displaystyle J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi}[\sigma(r^{\star}_{1}(s_{1},a_{1}),\ldots,r^{\star}_{H}(s_{H},a_{H}))].

This formulation is already a meaningful control problem before considering trajectory-level supervision (Zhang et al., 2020; Barakat et al., 2023). The agent still makes sequential decisions, and the environment admits local reward primitives, but the desired behavior may depend on how these primitives combine over the full trajectory. Such criteria arise naturally in long-horizon tasks, where forcing the objective into a cumulative reward can change the quantity one intends to optimize.

The outcome-based version is especially important because many datasets record this trajectory-level criterion directly. In this setting, the learner observes outcomes YY satisfying 𝔼⁡[Y∣τ]=R⁡(τ,r⋆)\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\tau]=R(\tau;r^{\star}), rather than the latent process rewards. Thus, the trajectory outcome is both the supervision signal and the optimization target. This makes the formulation more faithful to many real datasets, but also statistically more delicate: the learner must optimize a generalized objective from generalized trajectory-level supervision. This leads to a second, sharper question:

Is efficient learning still possible when both supervision and the objective are generalized?

In general, the answer is no. The clearest example is the all-success objective, where rewards are binary and R⁡(τ,r)=∏h=1Hrh​(sh,ah)R(\tau;r)=\prod_{h=1}^{H}r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h}), so a trajectory has value one only if every stage succeeds. We prove that, for this objective, any offline learner may require Ω⁡(2H)\Omega(2^{H}) trajectories to obtain nontrivial performance, even with deterministic transitions and constant state-action concentrability (Theorem 5).

This impossibility points to two distinct bottlenecks. The first is outcome aggregation: observing only R⁡(τ,r⋆)R(\tau;r^{\star}), a nonlinear σ\sigma may map different per-step reward processes to nearly indistinguishable trajectory outcomes. We quantify this inverse problem by the Reward Process Coefficient κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma) (Definition 1), which measures how well reward-process differences are preserved after aggregation. The second bottleneck comes from the generalized objective itself. To obtain a tractable theory, we restrict attention to aggregations that admit Bellman-style dynamic programming. Even then, generalized Bellman targets may further compress reward differences when forming one-step targets. We quantify this effect by the Bellman Inverse Coefficient χμ​(σ)\chi_{\mu}(\sigma) (Definition 2), which measures how well generalized Bellman targets preserve reward-process differences. With these two measures, we identify a tractable regime. Under structural assumptions, Generalized OPAC achieves suboptimality O~​(Vmax2​L​κμ​(σ)​H2​Cs​a​(π⋆)/n+Vmax2​L​χμ​(σ)​H4/n)\widetilde{O}\bigl(V_{\max}^{2}L\sqrt{\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma)H^{2}C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})/n}+V_{\max}^{2}L\sqrt{\chi_{\mu}(\sigma)H^{4}/n}\bigr) up to lower-order terms (Theorem 6). Thus the rate remains polynomial in the horizon, sample size, and offline concentrability, while κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma) and χμ​(σ)\chi_{\mu}(\sigma) track the two information-loss mechanisms above.

Our contributions

We study offline RL from trajectory-level supervision. First, for the standard cumulative-reward objective with scalar trajectory outcomes, we propose OPAC and prove matching upper and lower bounds up to logarithmic factors (Theorems 1 and 2), characterizing the cost of replacing step-level rewards by trajectory-level supervision. Second, we extend OPAC to trajectory preferences, with guarantees matching the leading horizon and concentrability dependence of the scalar-outcome setting (Theorem 3). Third, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study offline RL where both the supervision and the objective are generalized trajectory-level quantities: the observed outcome is a known aggregation of all stage-wise rewards, and the learning goal is to optimize this same quantity. In this setting, we prove an exponential impossibility result (Theorem 5) and identify a learnable regime through κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma) and χμ​(σ)\chi_{\mu}(\sigma), under which Generalized OPAC achieves polynomial sample complexity (Theorem 6).

2 Preliminary

Finite-horizon MDPs, policies, and occupancy

A finite-horizon Markov decision process is specified by M=(𝒮,𝒜,P,r⋆,H,s1)M=({\mathcal{S}},\mathcal{A},P,r^{\star},H,s_{1}), where: (i) H∈ℕ≥1H\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 1} is the horizon; (ii) 𝒮=⨆h=1H𝒮h{\mathcal{S}}=\bigsqcup_{h=1}^{H}{\mathcal{S}}_{h} and 𝒜=⨆h=1H𝒜h\mathcal{A}=\bigsqcup_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{A}_{h} are layered state and action spaces; (iii) P=(Ph)h=1H−1P=(P_{h})_{h=1}^{H-1}, with Ph:𝒮h×𝒜h→Δ⁡(𝒮h+1)P_{h}:{\mathcal{S}}_{h}\times\mathcal{A}_{h}\to\Delta({\mathcal{S}}_{h+1}), is the transition kernel; (iv) r⋆=(rh⋆)h=1Hr^{\star}=(r_{h}^{\star})_{h=1}^{H} is the unknown mean process reward, with rh⋆:𝒮h×𝒜h→[0,1]r_{h}^{\star}:{\mathcal{S}}_{h}\times\mathcal{A}_{h}\to[0,1]; and (v) s1∈𝒮1s_{1}\in{\mathcal{S}}_{1} is a fixed initial state. A trajectory is τ=(s1,a1,…,sH,aH)∈𝒮1×𝒜1×⋯×𝒮H×𝒜H\tau=(s_{1},a_{1},\dots,s_{H},a_{H})\in{\mathcal{S}}_{1}\times\mathcal{A}_{1}\times\cdots\times{\mathcal{S}}_{H}\times\mathcal{A}_{H}. The reward function is part of the environment and defines the optimization objective, but in our outcome-based setting the process-level rewards are not observed in the offline data. A Markov policy is π=(πh)h=1H\pi=(\pi_{h})_{h=1}^{H}, with πh:𝒮h→Δ⁡(𝒜h)\pi_{h}:{\mathcal{S}}_{h}\to\Delta(\mathcal{A}_{h}). We fix a policy class Π\Pi and denote the behavior policy used to collect data by μ∈Π\mu\in\Pi. For any π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, the step-hh state–action occupancy is dhπ(s,a)≔ℙτ∼π[(sh,ah)=(s,a)]d_{h}^{\pi}(s,a)\coloneqq\mathbb{P}_{\tau\sim\pi}\bigl[(s_{h},a_{h})=(s,a)\bigr], where τ∼π\tau\sim\pi denotes a rollout of π\pi from s1s_{1} under PP. We write 𝔼π​[⋅]=𝔼τ∼π​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\cdot]=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi}[\cdot] and 𝔼μ​[⋅]=𝔼τ∼μ​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\cdot]=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mu}[\cdot], and denote the step-hh occupancy of μ\mu by dhμd_{h}^{\mu}.

Cumulative rewards, values, objectives, and function classes

For any candidate mean process reward r=(rh)h=1Hr=(r_{h})_{h=1}^{H}, define the cumulative reward R⁡(τ,r)≔∑h=1Hrh​(sh,ah)R(\tau;r)\coloneqq\sum_{h=1}^{H}r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h}) and the step-hh QQ-function under π\pi by Qhπ,r​(s,a)≔𝔼π​[∑h′=hHrh′​(sh′,ah′)|(sh,ah)=(s,a)]Q_{h}^{\pi,r}(s,a)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{h^{\prime}=h}^{H}r_{h^{\prime}}(s_{h^{\prime}},a_{h^{\prime}})\,\Big|\,(s_{h},a_{h})=(s,a)\right], and let Vhπ,r(s)≔𝔼a∼πh(⋅∣s)[Qhπ,r(s,a)]V_{h}^{\pi,r}(s)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{h}(\cdot\mid s)}[Q_{h}^{\pi,r}(s,a)]. When r=r⋆r=r^{\star}, we omit it from the superscript and write Qhπ,VhπQ_{h}^{\pi},V_{h}^{\pi}, and set R⋆​(τ)≔R⁡(τ,r⋆)R^{\star}(\tau)\coloneqq R(\tau;r^{\star}). The policy value is J⁡(π)≔𝔼π​[R⋆​(τ)]=V1π​(s1)J(\pi)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[R^{\star}(\tau)]=V_{1}^{\pi}(s_{1}), and the in-class optimal comparator is π⋆∈argmaxπ∈ΠJ⁡(π)\pi^{\star}\in\mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}_{\pi\in\Pi}J(\pi). We are given a per-step value-function class ℱ=ℱ1×⋯×ℱH\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{F}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{F}_{H}, where ℱh⊆{f:𝒮h×𝒜h→[0,Vmax]}\mathcal{F}_{h}\subseteq\{f:{\mathcal{S}}_{h}\times\mathcal{A}_{h}\to[0,V_{\max}]\}, and a mean process-reward class ℛ⊆{r=(rh)h=1H:rh:𝒮h×𝒜h→[0,1]}\mathcal{R}\subseteq\{r=(r_{h})_{h=1}^{H}:r_{h}:{\mathcal{S}}_{h}\times\mathcal{A}_{h}\to[0,1]\}. We identify f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} with the tuple (f1,…,fH)(f_{1},\dots,f_{H}) and, since 𝒮h∩𝒮h′=∅{\mathcal{S}}_{h}\cap{\mathcal{S}}_{h^{\prime}}=\emptyset, also write f⁡(s,a)f(s,a) for fh​(s,a)f_{h}(s,a) whenever s∈𝒮hs\in{\mathcal{S}}_{h}.

Bellman operator

For a reward r=(rh)h=1Hr=(r_{h})_{h=1}^{H} and policy π\pi, the Bellman operator 𝒯rπ{\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi} acts on f:𝒮×𝒜→ℝf:{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R} by

(𝒯rπf)(s,a)≔rh(s,a)+𝔼s′∼Ph(⋅∣s,a)[fh+1(s′,π)],(s,a)∈𝒮h×𝒜h,\displaystyle({\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f)(s,a)\coloneqq r_{h}(s,a)+\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim P_{h}(\cdot\mid s,a)}\bigl[f_{h+1}(s^{\prime},\pi)\bigr],\qquad(s,a)\in{\mathcal{S}}_{h}\times\mathcal{A}_{h}, (1)

with the boundary convention fH+1≡0f_{H+1}\equiv 0, and we use the shorthand fh(s,π)≔𝔼a∼πh(⋅∣s)[fh(s,a)]f_{h}(s,\pi)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{h}(\cdot\mid s)}[f_{h}(s,a)]. When the reward subscript is omitted, 𝒯π≔𝒯r⋆π{\mathcal{T}}^{\pi}\coloneqq{\mathcal{T}}_{r^{\star}}^{\pi}.

Offline data and coverage

Unless stated otherwise, 𝒟={(τ(i),Y(i))}i=1n\mathcal{D}=\{(\tau^{(i)},Y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{n} denotes an offline dataset of nn i.i.d. trajectories τ(i)∼μ\tau^{(i)}\sim\mu, each annotated with a trajectory-level outcome Y(i)Y^{(i)} satisfying 𝔼⁡[Y(i)∣τ(i)]=R⋆​(τ(i))=∑h=1Hrh⋆​(sh(i),ah(i))\mathbb{E}[Y^{(i)}\mid\tau^{(i)}]=R^{\star}(\tau^{(i)})=\sum_{h=1}^{H}r_{h}^{\star}(s_{h}^{(i)},a_{h}^{(i)}). The precise observation model for Y(i)Y^{(i)} depends on the section. We write 𝔼𝒟​[ϕ⁡(τ,Y)]≔n−1​∑i=1nϕ⁡(τ(i),Y(i))\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\phi(\tau,Y)]\coloneqq n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\phi(\tau^{(i)},Y^{(i)}) for empirical averages.

The all-step state–action concentrability (Chen and Jiang, 2019; Xie et al., 2021a) of π∈Π\pi\in\Pi with respect to μ\mu is

Cs​a​(π)≔max⁡sup(s,a)∈𝒮h×𝒜hh∈[H]⁡dhπ​(s,a)dhμ​(s,a),\displaystyle C_{sa}(\pi)\coloneqq\max_{h\in[H]}\sup_{(s,a)\in{\mathcal{S}}_{h}\times\mathcal{A}_{h}}\frac{d_{h}^{\pi}(s,a)}{d_{h}^{\mu}(s,a)}, (2)

and Cs​aC_{sa} is always computed with respect to the fixed behavior policy μ\mu. This density-ratio condition is a standard coverage assumption in offline RL (Munos, 2007; Farahmand et al., 2010; Chen and Jiang, 2019). It could be relaxed to function-class-dependent coverage notions, where the density ratio is tested only against functions in the relevant class (Duan et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2021a; Song et al., 2022). Since this paper focuses on the granularity of reward supervision rather than coverage assumptions, we use the classical density-ratio formulation for simplicity.

Asymptotic notation

We use O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot), Ω⁡(⋅)\Omega(\cdot), and Θ⁡(⋅)\Theta(\cdot) for standard asymptotic bounds up to universal numerical constants. The notations O~​(⋅)\widetilde{O}(\cdot), Ω~​(⋅)\widetilde{\Omega}(\cdot), and Θ~​(⋅)\widetilde{\Theta}(\cdot) additionally hide factors polylogarithmic in the problem parameters, such as n,H,|𝒜|,|Π|,|ℱ|,|ℛ|n,H,|\mathcal{A}|,|\Pi|,|\mathcal{F}|,|\mathcal{R}|, and 1/δ1/\delta. Finally, a≲ba\lesssim b means a≤C​ba\leq Cb for a universal constant C>0C>0, and a≳ba\gtrsim b is defined analogously.

3 Sample-Efficient Offline RL with Outcome Reward

We work in the offline framework of Section 2, specializing to the case where each trajectory carries a single scalar label rather than process-level rewards, while the optimization target remains the standard expected cumulative return under r⋆r^{\star}. Thus, the learner observes only one unbiased cumulative-reward outcome after the trajectory terminates; it does not observe the reward vector (r1⋆​(s1,a1),…,rH⋆​(sH,aH))(r_{1}^{\star}(s_{1},a_{1}),\ldots,r_{H}^{\star}(s_{H},a_{H})) or any per-step reward labels. With rh⋆∈[0,1]r_{h}^{\star}\in[0,1], the latent cumulative return lies in [0,H][0,H]. In this section, we further assume Y(i)∈[0,H]Y^{(i)}\in[0,H] and set Vmax=HV_{\max}=H.

3.1 Algorithm

We define empirical criteria for policy mismatch, Bellman consistency under a candidate mean reward, and regression to scalar trajectory outcomes. Our proposed algorithm OPAC then alternates pessimistic evaluation with layer-wise exponential-weights policy updates.

Empirical criteria

Define yhr,f,π≔rh​(sh,ah)+fh+1​(sh+1,π)y_{h}^{r,f,\pi}\coloneqq r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})+f_{h+1}(s_{h+1},\pi) with the convention fH+1=0f_{H+1}=0, and

ℒ𝒟​(π,f)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}(\pi,f) ≔∑h=1H𝔼𝒟​[fh​(sh,π)−fh​(sh,ah)],\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\!\left[f_{h}(s_{h},\pi)-f_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})\right], (3a)
ℒ𝒟BE​(π,r,f)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{BE}}(\pi,r,f) ≔∑h=1H{𝔼𝒟​[(fh​(sh,ah)−yhr,f,π)2]−ming∈ℱh⁡𝔼𝒟​[(g⁡(sh,ah)−yhr,f,π)2]},\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{h=1}^{H}\left\{\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\!\left[\bigl(f_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})-y_{h}^{r,f,\pi}\bigr)^{2}\right]-\min_{g\in\mathcal{F}_{h}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\!\left[\bigl(g(s_{h},a_{h})-y_{h}^{r,f,\pi}\bigr)^{2}\right]\right\}, (3b)
ℒ𝒟RM​(r)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r) ≔𝔼𝒟​[(Y−∑h=1Hrh​(sh,ah))2].\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\!\left[\left(Y-\sum_{h=1}^{H}r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})\right)^{2}\right]. (3c)

The first term measures empirical policy mismatch, the second is a plug-in Bellman error under the candidate reward rr, and the third fits the latent process reward to the observed trajectory outcomes. The minimization over gg is the standard double-sampling correction for Bellman regression, removing the transition-noise variance from the squared target. Together, these criteria enforce Bellman consistency for the critic while anchoring the candidate reward to the outcome labels.

Outcome-based Pessimistic Actor-Critic (OPAC)

Fix η,β>0\eta,\beta>0 and K∈ℕK\in\mathbb{N}. Initialize π1,h(⋅∣s)=Unif(𝒜h)\pi_{1,h}(\cdot\mid s)=\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{A}_{h}). For k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K, perform

Pessimistic evaluation:(fk,rk)∈argmin(f,r)∈ℱ×ℛℒ𝒟(πk,f)+βℒ𝒟BE(πk,r,f)+βℒ𝒟RM(r),\displaystyle\textit{Pessimistic evaluation:}\quad(f_{k},r_{k})\in\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_{(f,r)\in\mathcal{F}\times\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}(\pi_{k},f)+\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{BE}}(\pi_{k},r,f)+\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r), (4)
Policy improvement:πk+1,h(⋅∣s)∝πk,h(⋅∣s)exp(fk,h(s,⋅)/η),h∈[H].\displaystyle\textit{Policy improvement:}\quad\pi_{k+1,h}(\cdot\mid s)\propto\pi_{k,h}(\cdot\mid s)\exp\bigl(f_{k,h}(s,\cdot)/\eta\bigr),\qquad h\in[H]. (5)

The output is the mixture policy π¯≔Unif⁡(π1,…,πK)\bar{\pi}\coloneqq\mathrm{Unif}(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{K}): at deployment, sample k∼Unif⁡[K]k\sim\mathrm{Unif}[K] once and execute πk\pi_{k} for the entire episode.

3.2 Theoretical Analysis

We state the assumptions and main upper bound for OPAC. Besides standard function-approximation conditions, the outcome-specific assumption is reward realizability.

Assumption 1 (Reward realizability).

The ground-truth mean process reward satisfies r⋆∈ℛr^{\star}\in\mathcal{R}.

We also assume approximate value realizability and Bellman completeness. The latter is imposed uniformly over candidate rewards r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}, since OPAC estimates rewards from outcome labels and evaluates Bellman backups under these candidates.

Assumption 2 (Approximate realizability).

For all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, min⁡suph,νf∈ℱ⁡‖fh−(𝒯r⋆π​f)h‖2,ν2≤εℱ\min_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\sup_{h,\nu}\|f_{h}-({\mathcal{T}}_{r^{\star}}^{\pi}f)_{h}\|_{2,\nu}^{2}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F}}.

Assumption 3 (Completeness).

For every (π,r,f)∈Π×ℛ×ℱ(\pi,r,f)\in\Pi\times\mathcal{R}\times\mathcal{F}, ming∈ℱ⁡‖g−𝒯rπ​f‖2,μ2≤εℱ,ℱ\min_{g\in\mathcal{F}}\|g-{\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f\|_{2,\mu}^{2}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}}.

Theorem 1 (Upper bound for outcome-based offline RL).

Suppose Assumptions 1, 2 and 3 hold. Running OPAC for KK iterations with suitable parameters η\eta and β\beta returns a policy π¯\bar{\pi} such that, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

J⁡(π⋆)−J⁡(π¯)=O~​(H2​Cs​a​(π⋆)n+H2K+H​Cs​a​(π⋆)​εℱ+H​Cs​a​(π⋆)​εℱ,ℱ+H​εℱ).\displaystyle J(\pi^{\star})-J(\bar{\pi})=\widetilde{O}\left(H^{2}\sqrt{\frac{C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})}{n}}+\frac{H^{2}}{\sqrt{K}}+\sqrt{HC_{sa}(\pi^{\star})\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F}}}+\sqrt{HC_{sa}(\pi^{\star})\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}}}+H\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F}}}\right). (6)

In particular, if εℱ=εℱ,ℱ=0\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F}}=\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}}=0 and K≥nK\geq n, then J⁡(π⋆)−J⁡(π¯)=O~​(H2​Cs​a​(π⋆)/n)J(\pi^{\star})-J(\bar{\pi})=\widetilde{O}\left(H^{2}\sqrt{{C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})}/{n}}\right), or equivalently n=O~​(H4​Cs​a​(π⋆)/ε2)n=\widetilde{O}(H^{4}C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})/\varepsilon^{2}) trajectories suffice for ε\varepsilon-optimality.

The proof of Theorem 1 is given in Appendix C. The terms in (6) have the usual interpretations: statistical error under coverage Cs​a​(π⋆)C_{sa}(\pi^{\star}), optimization error from KK actor–critic iterations, and approximation errors from εℱ\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F}} and εℱ,ℱ\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}}. The distinctive feature is the horizon dependence: relative to process-level supervision, outcome supervision pays one additional factor of HH. The lower bound in Theorem 2 shows that this factor is unavoidable, reflecting the statistical price of compressing HH process-level reward observations into a single trajectory outcome; see Remark 2.

3.3 Lower Bound

The next theorem matches scaling of Eq. 6, so ε\varepsilon-optimality can require Ω⁡(H4/ε2)\Omega(H^{4}/\varepsilon^{2}) trajectories.

Theorem 2 (Lower bound for outcome-based offline RL).

For all sufficiently large horizons HH and all n≥64​H2n\geq 64H^{2}, there exists a class of outcome-based offline RL instances with deterministic transitions and Cs​a​(π⋆)≤2C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})\leq 2, such that any algorithm using nn trajectories must incur

supM𝔼M​[JM​(πM⋆)−JM​(π^)]≥c​H2n,\displaystyle\sup_{M}\mathbb{E}_{M}\left[J_{M}(\pi_{M}^{\star})-J_{M}(\widehat{\pi})\right]\geq c\frac{H^{2}}{\sqrt{n}},

for a universal constant c>0c>0. Thus, even with constant state–action coverage and no transition-learning difficulty, achieving expected sub-optimality at most ε\varepsilon requires Ω⁡(H4/ε2)\Omega\left(H^{4}/\varepsilon^{2}\right) trajectories.

The proof of Theorem 2 is given in Section E.1.

Remark 1 (Tightness of OPAC).

Theorem 2 matches Theorem 1 in every parameter that appears: the H2H^{2} horizon factor, the 1/n\sqrt{1/n} statistical rate, and the dependence on Cs​a​(π⋆)C_{sa}(\pi^{\star}). Consequently, the O~​(H2​Cs​a​(π⋆)/n)\widetilde{O}(H^{2}\sqrt{C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})/n}) guarantee achieved by OPAC—through pessimistic actor–critic search and trajectory-level squared regression on the outcome label—is statistically optimal up to logarithmic factors among all algorithms that observe bounded unbiased outcome labels. No refinement of these algorithmic ingredients can improve the rate without strengthening the supervision model itself.

Remark 2 (Comparison with process-supervision offline RL).

Taken together, Theorems 1 and 2 identify Θ~​(H4/ε2)\widetilde{\Theta}(H^{4}/\varepsilon^{2}) trajectories as the outcome-supervised sample complexity. This is strictly more demanding than the process-level setting, where rewards are observed at every step: Xie et al. (2021b) establish an information-theoretic lower bound of Ω⁡(H3/ε2)\Omega(H^{3}/\varepsilon^{2}) for that regime. The hard instance in Theorem 2 has essentially no transition-learning difficulty—it is a deterministic chain with a single state per layer, two actions, and a constant single-policy concentrability coefficient. The extra factor of HH therefore cannot be attributed to exploration, transition uncertainty, or poor coverage; it is the purely statistical price of compressing HH per-step reward signals into a single trajectory-level label.

4 Offline RL from Trajectory-Level Preferences

We next consider a weaker form of trajectory-level supervision: instead of a scalar outcome for each trajectory, the learner observes only pairwise preferences between trajectories. This is the offline analogue of the preference-based outcome-feedback model studied by Chen et al. (2025), and also a stylized abstraction of reward modeling in RLHF. Throughout this section, we keep the normalization rh⋆​(s,a)∈[0,1]r_{h}^{\star}(s,a)\in[0,1], so R⋆​(τ)∈[0,H]R^{\star}(\tau)\in[0,H]. The optimization target remains the standard cumulative return; only the observation model changes.

Preference observation model

The offline dataset is 𝒟Pref={(τ(i),+,τ(i),−,y(i))}i=1n\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{Pref}}=\{(\tau^{(i),+},\tau^{(i),-},y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{n}, where τ(i),+,τ(i),−∼i.i.d.μ\tau^{(i),+},\tau^{(i),-}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mu and y(i)∈{0,1}y^{(i)}\in\{0,1\} indicates whether the first trajectory is preferred. We assume a Bradley–Terry–Luce (BTL) comparison model (Bradley and Terry, 1952; Christiano et al., 2017). For any reward r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}, define

Cr​(τ+,τ−)≔exp⁡(γ​R​(τ+,r))exp⁡(γ​R​(τ+,r))+exp⁡(γ​R​(τ−,r)),\displaystyle\mathrm{C}_{r}(\tau^{+},\tau^{-})\coloneqq\frac{\exp(\gamma R(\tau^{+};r))}{\exp(\gamma R(\tau^{+};r))+\exp(\gamma R(\tau^{-};r))}, (7)

where γ>0\gamma>0 is fixed. Preferences are generated from the true reward:

y(i)|(τ(i),+,τ(i),−)∼Bern⁡(Cr⋆​(τ(i),+,τ(i),−)).\displaystyle y^{(i)}\mid(\tau^{(i),+},\tau^{(i),-})\sim\mathrm{Bern}\bigl(\mathrm{C}_{r^{\star}}(\tau^{(i),+},\tau^{(i),-})\bigr). (8)

Thus the learner observes neither r⋆r^{\star} nor R⋆​(τ)R^{\star}(\tau) directly, but only noisy binary comparisons.

Preference loss and algorithm

For a candidate reward r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}, define the empirical preference loss

ℒ𝒟PrefPref​(r)≔1n​∑i=1n[−y(i)​log⁡Cr​(τ(i),+,τ(i),−)−(1−y(i))​log⁡(1−Cr​(τ(i),+,τ(i),−))].\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{Pref}}}^{\mathrm{Pref}}(r)\coloneqq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[-y^{(i)}\log\mathrm{C}_{r}(\tau^{(i),+},\tau^{(i),-})-(1-y^{(i)})\log\bigl(1-\mathrm{C}_{r}(\tau^{(i),+},\tau^{(i),-})\bigr)\right]. (9)

This replaces the squared reward-model loss ℒ𝒟RM​(r)\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r) in Equation 3c: both fit the latent per-step reward from trajectory feedback, but preferences identify rewards only through return differences. Uniform shifts of all trajectory returns are therefore unidentifiable, but do not affect policy optimization.

Let 𝒟traj\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{traj}} denote the 2​n2n individual trajectories appearing in the preference pairs. Preference-based OPAC uses the same pessimistic actor–critic template as OPAC, with only the reward-model loss changed. Specifically, starting from the same uniform policy π1\pi_{1}, for k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K compute

(fk,rk)∈argmin(f,r)∈ℱ×ℛℒ𝒟traj​(πk,f)+β​ℒ𝒟trajBE​(πk,r,f)+β​ℒ𝒟PrefPref​(r),\displaystyle(f_{k},r_{k})\in\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_{(f,r)\in\mathcal{F}\times\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{traj}}}(\pi_{k},f)+\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{traj}}}^{\mathrm{BE}}(\pi_{k},r,f)+\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{Pref}}}^{\mathrm{Pref}}(r), (10)

and then apply the same layer-wise exponential-weights policy update as in Equation 5. The output is again the mixture policy π¯=Unif⁡(π1,…,πK)\bar{\pi}=\mathrm{Unif}(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{K}). Thus, the preference setting requires no new actor–critic machinery: only the reward-fitting changes from squared regression to logistic regression.

Sample complexity

Assume every candidate reward r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R} satisfies 0≤rh​(s,a)≤10\leq r_{h}(s,a)\leq 1, so R⁡(τ,r)∈[0,H]R(\tau;r)\in[0,H], and set Vmax=HV_{\max}=H as in the scalar-outcome setting. We regard the BTL model as fixed; the comparison constants αC\alpha_{\mathrm{C}} and cCc_{\mathrm{C}} are defined in Equation 66.

Theorem 3 (Upper bound for outcome-based offline RL with preferences).

Suppose Assumptions 1, 2 and 3 hold. Running preference-based OPAC for KK iterations with suitable parameters η\eta and β\beta returns a policy π¯\bar{\pi} such that, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

J⁡(π⋆)−J⁡(π¯)=O~​(CLOSE\displaystyle J(\pi^{\star})-J(\bar{\pi})=\widetilde{O}\Bigg( 1+1αC​[H2​Cs​a​(π⋆)n+cC​H​Cs​a​(π⋆)n]\displaystyle\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{\alpha_{\mathrm{C}}}}\left[H^{2}\sqrt{\frac{C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})}{n}}+\sqrt{\frac{c_{\mathrm{C}}HC_{sa}(\pi^{\star})}{n}}\right]
OPEN+H​Cs​a​(π⋆)​εℱ+H​Cs​a​(π⋆)​εℱ,ℱ+H2K+H​εℱ).\displaystyle\quad+\sqrt{HC_{sa}(\pi^{\star})\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F}}}+\sqrt{HC_{sa}(\pi^{\star})\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}}}+\frac{H^{2}}{\sqrt{K}}+H\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F}}}\Bigg). (11)

In particular, if εℱ=εℱ,ℱ=0\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F}}=\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}}=0 and K≥nK\geq n, then

J⁡(π⋆)−J⁡(π¯)=O~​(1+1/αC​[H2​Cs​a​(π⋆)/n+cC​H​Cs​a​(π⋆)/n]).J(\pi^{\star})-J(\bar{\pi})=\widetilde{O}\left(\sqrt{1+1/\alpha_{\mathrm{C}}}\left[H^{2}\sqrt{C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})/n}+\sqrt{c_{\mathrm{C}}HC_{sa}(\pi^{\star})/n}\right]\right).

The proof is given in Appendix D. The rate has the same offline-RL structure as Theorem 1: the coverage coefficient Cs​a​(π⋆)C_{sa}(\pi^{\star}), and the leading term preserves the H2​Cs​a​(π⋆)/nH^{2}\sqrt{C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})/n} dependence. The additional constants αC\alpha_{\mathrm{C}} and cCc_{\mathrm{C}} quantify the comparison model on the bounded return range [0,H][0,H].

5 Outcome-Based RL with Generalized Objective

The preceding sections fix the cumulative-reward objective and weaken only the supervision, replacing the scalar trajectory outcome by a binary preference. In many applications, however, the trajectory-level signal is not a noisy proxy for a latent per-step sum but the performance criterion itself, and this criterion may be a nonlinear function of the per-step rewards. The natural object of study is then the trajectory outcome itself, both as the data we observe and as the quantity we wish to maximize.

This motivates the following generalized RL formulation. Fix a known stage-wise aggregation rule σ:ℝH→[0,Vmax]\sigma:\mathbb{R}^{H}\to[0,V_{\max}]. For any trajectory τ=(s1,a1,…,sH,aH)\tau=(s_{1},a_{1},\dots,s_{H},a_{H}) and any candidate per-step reward r=(rh)h=1H∈ℛr=(r_{h})_{h=1}^{H}\in\mathcal{R}, define the trajectory return R⁡(τ,r)=σ⁡(r1​(s1,a1),…,rH​(sH,aH))R(\tau;r)=\sigma\bigl(r_{1}(s_{1},a_{1}),\ldots,r_{H}(s_{H},a_{H})\bigr) and the corresponding policy value11 1 In this section we overload notations, but just extend from the classical setting to the generalized objective setting.

J⁡(π)=𝔼τ∼π​[R⁡(τ,r⋆)]=𝔼τ∼π​[σ⁡(r1⋆​(s1,a1),…,rH⋆​(sH,aH))].\displaystyle J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi}[R(\tau;r^{\star})]=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi}\left[\sigma\bigl(r^{\star}_{1}(s_{1},a_{1}),\ldots,r^{\star}_{H}(s_{H},a_{H})\bigr)\right]. (12)

Taking σ\sigma to be the sum recovers the classical setting; other choices capture nonlinear trajectory criteria, such as the following all-success outcome.

Example 4 (All-success outcome).

Suppose rh​(s,a)∈{0,1}r_{h}(s,a)\in\{0,1\}, and let σ⁡(u1,…,uH)=∏h=1Huh.\sigma(u_{1},\ldots,u_{H})=\prod_{h=1}^{H}u_{h}. Then R⁡(τ,r)=∏h=1Hrh​(sh,ah)=1R(\tau;r)=\prod_{h=1}^{H}r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})=1 if every stage succeeds, so the generalized objective J⁡(π)=𝔼τ∼π​[∏h=1Hrh⋆​(sh,ah)]J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi}\left[\prod_{h=1}^{H}r_{h}^{\star}(s_{h},a_{h})\right] is the probability of completing the trajectory without any failed stage.

The offline dataset takes the same form as before, 𝒟={(τ(i),Y(i))}i=1n\mathcal{D}=\{(\tau^{(i)},Y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{n}, with 𝔼⁡[Y(i)∣τ(i)]=R⁡(τ(i),r⋆)\mathbb{E}[Y^{(i)}\mid\tau^{(i)}]=R(\tau^{(i)};r^{\star}) and Y(i)∈[0,Vmax]Y^{(i)}\in[0,V_{\max}]. The learner is asked to use 𝒟\mathcal{D} to maximize Eq. 12. We assume that the trajectory return R⁡(τ,r)R(\tau;r) and every value function fh∈ℱf_{h}\in\mathcal{F} take values in [0,Vmax][0,V_{\max}].

Remark 3.

The generalized objective is well posed under process supervision, and the standard machinery of value functions and Bellman optimality equations extends to this setting (Appendix F). Under outcome-based supervision, the interpretation is especially direct: maximizing Equation 12 is exactly maximizing the expected trajectory outcome recorded in the offline data.

Unfortunately, this problem is no longer learnable in general. We first give an impossibility result for Example 4: even with deterministic transitions and constant state–action concentrability, the outcome label is informative on only an exponentially small set of trajectories, which forces an exponential sample complexity.

Theorem 5 (Exponential lower bound under all-success aggregation).

For any horizon H≥1H\geq 1, there exists a family of deterministic finite-horizon MDPs with the all-success outcome in Example 4 and state–action concentrability Cs​a​(π⋆)≤2C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})\leq 2, such that any offline learner using nn i.i.d. outcome-labeled trajectories satisfies infπ^sup𝛉∈{0,1}H𝔼⁡[J𝛉​(π𝛉⋆)−J𝛉​(π^)]≥14​(1−n⋅21−H)\inf_{\widehat{\pi}}\sup_{{\bm{\theta}}\in\{0,1\}^{H}}\mathbb{E}[J_{\bm{\theta}}(\pi^{\star}_{\bm{\theta}})-J_{\bm{\theta}}(\widehat{\pi})]\geq\frac{1}{4}(1-n\cdot 2^{1-H}). In particular, achieving expected suboptimality below 1/81/8 requires Ω⁡(2H)\Omega(2^{H}) trajectories.

The proof is given in Section E.2. It shows that, without suitable structure on σ\sigma, outcome-based learning can be statistically intractable. We therefore focus on structured aggregations. The first requirement is that the loss of per-step reward information in the scalar outcome is controlled by the reward-process coefficient κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma) in Definition 1. The second requirement is that the generalized objective admits a Bellman-learnable aggregation, with the Bellman inverse coefficient χμ​(σ)\chi_{\mu}(\sigma) in Definition 2 measuring how much per-step information is preserved by the Bellman operator.

Definition 1 (Reward Process Coefficient).

For an aggregation σ\sigma and a distribution μ\mu, define

κμ​(σ)≔supr≠r′∑h=1H𝔼μ​[(rh−rh′)2​(sh,ah)]𝔼τ∼μ​[(R⁡(τ,r)−R⁡(τ,r′))2].\displaystyle\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma)\coloneqq\sup_{r\neq r^{\prime}}\frac{\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\bigl[(r_{h}-r^{\prime}_{h})^{2}(s_{h},a_{h})\bigr]}{\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mu}\bigl[(R(\tau;r)-R(\tau;r^{\prime}))^{2}\bigr]}.

The coefficient κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma) measures how hard it is to recover per-step rewards from outcome signals: a large κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma) means that distinct reward profiles look nearly identical after being aggregated by σ\sigma.

Next, we represent R⁡(τ,r)R(\tau;r) through stage-wise maps σh\sigma_{h}. For τ=(s1,a1,…,sH,aH)\tau=(s_{1},a_{1},\ldots,s_{H},a_{H}), let τh=(sh,ah,…,sH,aH)\tau_{h}=(s_{h},a_{h},\ldots,s_{H},a_{H}) denote the trajectory truncated at stage hh, and Rh​(τh,r)R_{h}(\tau_{h};r) denote the return from stage hh onward, so that R⁡(τ,r)=R1​(τ1,r)R(\tau;r)=R_{1}(\tau_{1};r). We define Rh​(τh,r)R_{h}(\tau_{h};r) recursively through stage-wise aggregation functions σh:ℝ×ℝ→ℝ\sigma_{h}:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} and a terminal constant g∈ℝg\in\mathbb{R}, where σh​(u,v)\sigma_{h}(u,v) aggregates the current per-step reward uu with the continuation return vv from stage hh onward:

RH+1≔g,Rh​(τh,r)\displaystyle R_{H+1}\coloneqq g,\quad R_{h}(\tau_{h};r) ≔σh(rh(sh,ah),Rh+1(τh+1;r)),h=H,…,1.\displaystyle\coloneqq\sigma_{h}\bigl(r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h}),R_{h+1}(\tau_{h+1};r)\bigr),\qquad h=H,\ldots,1. (13)

Generalized Bellman operator

Given a policy π\pi, candidate reward r=(rh)h=1H∈ℛr=(r_{h})_{h=1}^{H}\in\mathcal{R}, and value function f=(fh)h=1H∈ℱf=(f_{h})_{h=1}^{H}\in\mathcal{F}, define the generalized Bellman operator 𝒯rπ{\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi} by

(𝒯rπf)h(s,a)≔σh(rh(s,a),𝔼s′∼Ph(⋅∣s,a)[fh+1(s′,π)]),(s,a)∈𝒮h×𝒜h,\displaystyle({\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f)_{h}(s,a)\coloneqq\sigma_{h}\bigl(r_{h}(s,a),\,\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim P_{h}(\cdot\mid s,a)}[f_{h+1}(s^{\prime},\pi)]\bigr),\qquad(s,a)\in{\mathcal{S}}_{h}\times\mathcal{A}_{h}, (14)

with boundary convention fH+1​(⋅,π)≡gf_{H+1}(\cdot,\pi)\equiv g. When r=r⋆r=r^{\star}, we write 𝒯π≔𝒯r⋆π{\mathcal{T}}^{\pi}\coloneqq{\mathcal{T}}_{r^{\star}}^{\pi}.

Definition 2 (Bellman Inverse Coefficient).

For aggregation σ\sigma and trajectory distribution μ\mu, define

χμ​(σ)≔supπ,f,r≠r′∑h=1H𝔼μ​[(rh−rh′)2​(sh,ah)]∑h=1H𝔼μ​[((𝒯rπ​f)h−(𝒯r′π​f)h)2​(sh,ah)].\displaystyle\chi_{\mu}(\sigma)\coloneqq\sup_{\pi,f,r\neq r^{\prime}}\frac{\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\bigl[(r_{h}-r^{\prime}_{h})^{2}(s_{h},a_{h})\bigr]}{\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\bigl[(({\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f)_{h}-({\mathcal{T}}_{r^{\prime}}^{\pi}f)_{h})^{2}(s_{h},a_{h})\bigr]}.

The coefficient χμ​(σ)\chi_{\mu}(\sigma) measures how much Bellman targets can compress reward differences: smaller χ\chi means that closeness of Bellman targets more tightly controls closeness of the underlying rewards.

Remark 4 (Why two coefficients are necessary).

The Reward Process Coefficient κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma) and the Bellman Inverse Coefficient χμ​(σ)\chi_{\mu}(\sigma) capture two distinct inverse problems that any outcome-based generalized RL algorithm must address. The coefficient κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma) governs information loss on the data side: it measures how well the scalar trajectory outcome R⁡(τ,r⋆)R(\tau;r^{\star}) identifies the latent per-step reward process r⋆r^{\star} through the aggregation rule σ\sigma. In particular, the statistical complexity of learning per-step rewards from trajectory outcomes is precisely captured by κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma), as detailed in Appendix I. The coefficient χμ​(σ)\chi_{\mu}(\sigma) governs information loss on the dynamic-programming side: it measures how well generalized Bellman targets preserve and propagate reward differences during policy optimization.

Both coefficients appear in the rate of Theorem 6 because Generalized OPAC must solve both tasks: it must recover the latent reward process from outcome labels, controlled by κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma), and optimize the generalized objective through Bellman-style dynamic programming, controlled by χμ​(σ)\chi_{\mu}(\sigma). These two roles are independent and cannot be merged into a single quantity. In simpler settings, one of the two coefficients may become unnecessary. With process supervision, the outcome inverse problem disappears, so κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma) is not needed. For the standard cumulative-reward objective, χμ​(σ)≡1\chi_{\mu}(\sigma)\equiv 1, since per-step reward differences pass through the Bellman operator without additional compression.

We further restrict σh​(u,v)\sigma_{h}(u,v) to satisfy the following regularity Assumption 4, which is not meant to characterize all trajectory-level objectives; rather, it identifies a Bellman-learnable subclass for which outcome-based generalized offline RL is statistically tractable. Cumulative returns use σh​(u,v)=u+v\sigma_{h}(u,v)=u+v with g=0g=0; all-success (Example 4) uses σh​(u,v)=u​v\sigma_{h}(u,v)=uv with g=1g=1. Appendix H presents additional objectives and relates statistical difficulty to κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma) and χμ​(σ)\chi_{\mu}(\sigma).

Assumption 4.
(1) Affine in vv: σh​(u,v)=ah​(u)​v+bh​(u)\sigma_{h}(u,v)=a_{h}(u)v+b_{h}(u).22 2 Affine dependence on vv is necessary for 𝔼v​[σh​(u,v)]=σh​(u,𝔼​v)\mathbb{E}_{v}[\sigma_{h}(u,v)]=\sigma_{h}(u,\mathbb{E}v) to hold for every law of vv. (2) No expansion of the continuation: ah​(u)∈[0,1]a_{h}(u)\in[0,1]. (3) ah,bha_{h},b_{h}are LL-Lipschitz in uu. (4) For every f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, hh, and (s,a)(s,a), with vh(s,a)=𝔼s′∼Ph(⋅∣s,a)[Vh+1π,f(s′)]v_{h}(s,a)=\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim P_{h}(\cdot\mid s,a)}[V_{h+1}^{\pi,f}(s^{\prime})], there exists r~h​(s,a)\tilde{r}_{h}(s,a) such that σh​(r~h​(s,a),vh​(s,a))=fh​(s,a)\sigma_{h}(\tilde{r}_{h}(s,a),v_{h}(s,a))=f_{h}(s,a).

Empirical criteria and generalized OPAC

We now instantiate OPAC for the generalized objective. The actor–critic structure is unchanged; only the Bellman target, reward loss, and trajectory weights are adapted. Define the generalized one-step target yhr,f,π≔σh​(rh​(sh,ah),fh+1​(sh+1,π))y_{h}^{r,f,\pi}\coloneqq\sigma_{h}(r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h}),f_{h+1}(s_{h+1},\pi)) for h=1,…,Hh=1,\ldots,H, with the convention fH+1=gf_{H+1}=g. For the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, define

ℒ𝒟Wr​(π,r,f)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{W^{r}}(\pi,r,f) ≔∑h=1H𝔼𝒟​[Whr​(τ)​(fh​(sh,π)−fh​(sh,ah))],\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\!\left[W_{h}^{r}(\tau)\bigl(f_{h}(s_{h},\pi)-f_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})\bigr)\right], (15a)
ℒ𝒟BE​(π,r,f)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{BE}}(\pi,r,f) ≔∑h=1H{𝔼𝒟​[(fh​(sh,ah)−yhr,f,π)2]−minf′∈ℱh⁡𝔼𝒟​[(f′​(sh,ah)−yhr,f,π)2]},\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{h=1}^{H}\left\{\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\!\left[\bigl(f_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})-y_{h}^{r,f,\pi}\bigr)^{2}\right]-\min_{f^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}_{h}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\!\left[\bigl(f^{\prime}(s_{h},a_{h})-y_{h}^{r,f,\pi}\bigr)^{2}\right]\right\}, (15b)
ℒ𝒟RM​(r)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r) ≔𝔼𝒟​[(R⁡(τ,r)−Y)2].\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\!\left[\bigl(R(\tau;r)-Y\bigr)^{2}\right]. (15c)

Here W1r≡1W_{1}^{r}\equiv 1 and Whr​(τ)≔∏j=1h−1aj​(rj​(sj,aj))W_{h}^{r}(\tau)\coloneqq\prod_{j=1}^{h-1}a_{j}(r_{j}(s_{j},a_{j})) for h∈[H]h\in[H].

Generalized OPAC uses the same policy initialization, layer-wise exponential-weights update, and mixture output π¯≔Unif⁡(π1,…,πK)\bar{\pi}\coloneqq\mathrm{Unif}(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{K}) as OPAC. The only change is the pessimistic evaluation step: for k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K, compute

(fk,rk)∈argmin(f,r)∈ℱ×ℛℒ𝒟Wr​(πk,r,f)+β​ℒ𝒟BE​(πk,r,f)+β​ℒ𝒟RM​(r),\displaystyle(f_{k},r_{k})\in\mathop{\mathrm{argmin}}_{(f,r)\in\mathcal{F}\times\mathcal{R}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{W^{r}}(\pi_{k},r,f)+\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{BE}}(\pi_{k},r,f)+\beta\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r), (16)

then apply the same policy-improvement step as in Equation 5.

Theorem 6 (Sample complexity of generalized OPAC).

Suppose that Assumptions 1, 2, 3 and 4 hold. Running generalized OPAC for KK iterations with suitable parameters η\eta and β\beta returns a policy π¯\bar{\pi} such that, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

J⁡(π⋆)−J⁡(π¯)≤O~​(CLOSE\displaystyle J(\pi^{\star})-J(\bar{\pi})\leq\widetilde{O}\!\Bigl( Vmax2​L​κμ​(σ)​H2​Cs​a​(π⋆)n+Vmax2​L​χμ​(σ)​H4n+Vmax​H​log⁡|𝒜|K\displaystyle V_{\max}^{2}L\sqrt{\frac{\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma)H^{2}C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})}{n}}+V_{\max}^{2}L\sqrt{\frac{\chi_{\mu}(\sigma)H^{4}}{n}}+V_{\max}H\sqrt{\frac{\log|\mathcal{A}|}{K}} (17)
OPEN+Φ​εℱ,ℱ+(Φ+H2)​εℱ)\displaystyle+\Phi\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}}}+(\Phi+H^{2})\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F}}}\Bigr)

where Φ=O~​(L​Vmax​κμ​(σ)​H​Cs​a​(π⋆)+Vmax​L​χμ​(σ)​H3+H​Cs​a​(π⋆))\Phi=\widetilde{O}\bigl(LV_{\max}\sqrt{\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma)HC_{sa}(\pi^{\star})}+V_{\max}L\sqrt{\chi_{\mu}(\sigma)H^{3}}+\sqrt{HC_{sa}(\pi^{\star})}\bigr).

The proof of Theorem 6 is given in Appendix G. The dependence on the aggregation map σ\sigma separates into two complementary bottlenecks, captured by κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma) and χμ​(σ)\chi_{\mu}(\sigma) (Definitions 1 and 2): outcome aggregation may obscure the latent per-step rewards, while generalized Bellman propagation may further compress reward differences when forming one-step targets.

6 Conclusion

We developed a sample-complexity theory for offline RL with trajectory-level supervision. For cumulative-reward objectives, OPAC achieves a sharp O~​(H2​Cs​a​(π⋆)/n)\widetilde{O}(H^{2}\sqrt{C_{sa}(\pi^{\star})/n}) rate, showing the statistical cost of compressing HH process-level rewards into one trajectory-level label. The same template extends to trajectory preferences. For nonlinear trajectory aggregations, we show an exponential barrier in general, and polynomial sample complexity for structured aggregations controlled by κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma) and χμ​(σ)\chi_{\mu}(\sigma). Together, these results delineate when trajectory-level supervision enables efficient offline policy optimization and when missing process-level rewards are fundamentally restrictive.

Limitations.

Our generalized framework assumes a known aggregation rule with Bellman-style structure, and does not fully characterize which trajectory-level objectives are both statistically learnable and practically meaningful. Identifying broader structural conditions for efficient outcome-based learning remains an important direction.

Appendix

Appendix A Related Work

Offline RL Theory

Our work builds on a rich body of theoretical results in offline RL; see Jiang and Xie (2025) for a recent survey. A central principle is pessimism in the face of uncertainty, which counteracts distribution shift by penalizing value estimates in regions poorly covered by data (Yin and Wang, 2021; Jin et al., 2021b; Rashidinejad et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2021a; Cheng et al., 2022; Blanchet et al., 2023). Closely related to our algorithmic approach are pessimistic and adversarially trained actor-critic methods for offline RL (Xie et al., 2021a; Zanette et al., 2021; Cheng et al., 2022; Ji et al., 2024). On the data coverage side, recent works have progressively weakened the required assumptions from all-policy concentrability to single-policy concentrability and partial coverage, with the minimax optimal sample complexity of model-based offline RL now settled (Rashidinejad et al., 2021; Xie et al., 2021a; Xie et al., 2021b; Zhan et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024). On the function approximation side, a key question is what structural conditions on the function class enable efficient learning, spanning realizability-only guarantees, unifying complexity measures such as the Bellman eluder dimension, fundamental impossibility results, instance-dependent bounds, and characterizations of inherent Bellman error (Xie and Jiang, 2021; Jin et al., 2021a; Foster et al., 2021; Nguyen-Tang et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2023; Golowich and Moitra, 2024).

Preference Learning

A complementary line of theoretical work studies RL from preference feedback rather than scalar rewards. Empirically, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) (Christiano et al., 2017) has become a central recipe for aligning large generative models, and direct preference optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023) reformulates the RLHF objective as a supervised loss on preference data. On the theoretical side, Zhu et al. (2023) provide principled guarantees for RLHF under both pairwise and KK-wise comparison models, Xiong et al. (2024) bridge theory and practice for iterative preference learning under KL regularization, and Zhan et al. (2023) establish provable guarantees for offline preference-based RL. Our preference setting in Section 4 adopts the standard Bradley–Terry–Luce comparison model (Bradley and Terry, 1952; Christiano et al., 2017) and operates entirely in the offline regime. Compared with these prior analyses, we maintain dependence on a single-policy state–action concentrability Cs​a​(π⋆)C_{sa}(\pi^{\star}) rather than the trajectory-level concentrability that often appears in preference-based analyses, and our guarantee depends on the BTL model only through interpretable constants αC\alpha_{\mathrm{C}} and cCc_{\mathrm{C}} that capture preference identifiability and concentration on bounded return ranges.

Outcome-based RL

Outcome-based RL—where the learner observes only trajectory-level signals rather than per-step rewards—has been studied under several names. A long theoretical line on aggregate / trajectory / bandit feedback (Neu and Bartók, 2013; Efroni et al., 2021; Chatterji et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022; Cassel et al., 2024; Lancewicki and Mansour, 2025) considers learners that receive only an episode-level reward, primarily in online tabular or linear MDP settings. A second, more recent line studies outcome supervision under general function approximation, motivated by reasoning datasets and human-feedback alignment in large language models (Stiennon et al., 2020; Cobbe et al., 2021; Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022; Jaech et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025): Jia et al. (2025) show that offline outcome data can be transformed into per-step pseudo-rewards via trajectory-level regression at a cost controlled by the single-policy state–action concentrability rather than the much larger trajectory-level concentrability; Yuan et al. (2025) propose trajectory Bellman residual minimization for LLM reasoning and improved the change-of-trajectory-measure inequality that we adopt which is initially introduced by Jia et al. (2025); and Chen et al. (2025) establish an online optimism-based algorithm with O~​(Ccov​H3/ε2)\widetilde{O}(C_{\mathrm{cov}}H^{3}/\varepsilon^{2}) sample complexity together with an exponential outcome-versus-process separation. Outcome-level feedback is also implicit in goal-reaching with sparse rewards (Andrychowicz et al., 2017), in clinical and healthcare RL where labels are revealed only at trajectory boundaries (Komorowski et al., 2018; Gottesman et al., 2019), and in trajectory-level human preferences (covered separately below). Compared to these works, we focus on the offline regime under partial (single-policy) coverage and additionally study generalized (nonlinear) trajectory-level objectives, where outcome-based learning may be statistically intractable and requires new complexity measures.

Compared with PRM Methods

A rapidly growing empirical literature trains reward models that score either intermediate steps (process reward models, PRMs) or completed trajectories (outcome reward models, ORMs), particularly for verifying language-model reasoning (Lightman et al., 2023; Uesato et al., 2022). Uesato et al. (2022) compare process- and outcome-based feedback at scale on math word problems, while Lightman et al. (2023) report that step-by-step process supervision can outperform outcome supervision on challenging math benchmarks. Jia et al. (2025) subsequently provide a theoretical perspective showing that, under suitable coverage and realizability conditions, outcome supervision can match process supervision up to polynomial-in-horizon factors, suggesting that the empirical gap may stem from algorithmic rather than purely statistical sources. Our results sharpen this picture in the offline setting through matched upper and lower bounds: we precisely quantify the statistical price of outcome supervision as a single extra horizon factor relative to the process-supervised lower bound of Xie et al. (2021b), arising purely from compressing HH per-step signals into a single label. We further extend this analysis to BTL preferences and to nonlinear trajectory-level objectives, where the picture changes qualitatively: structured aggregations remain tractable through the complexity measures we introduce, whereas certain nonlinear outcomes (e.g., all-success) admit exponential lower bounds even under constant state–action coverage.

Generalized RL Objectives

Different optimization objectives correspond to different ways of aggregating stage-wise signals into trajectory-level criteria. Theoretical lines in this direction include risk-sensitive RL (Howard and Matheson, 1972; Bastani et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a; Han et al., 2025), planning with submodular or other general (e.g., permutation-symmetric) trajectory objectives (Wang et al., 2020a; Wang et al., 2020b), max-reward RL that replaces the cumulative return by the maximum per-step reward (Quah and Quek, 2006; Gottipati et al., 2020; Veviurko et al., 2024), dynamic-programming foundations for non-cumulative objectives that introduce parallel notions of generalized reward aggregation, value functions, and Bellman operators (Cui and Yu, 2023), optimization of state–action occupancy utilities beyond cumulative rewards under hidden convexity or general utilities where Bellman dynamic programming breaks down (Zhang et al., 2020; Barakat et al., 2023), control synthesis from linear temporal logic specifications (Bozkurt et al., 2020; Bagatella et al., 2024), and PAC learnability for computably continuous RL objectives (Yang et al., 2023). Most of these works analyze convergence of dynamic-programming or online policy-gradient procedures rather than offline finite-sample complexity.

Generalized aggregations also arise naturally in language-model post-training and reasoning, mirroring the examples in Appendix H. Process- and outcome-supervised reward modeling for math reasoning (Cobbe et al., 2021; Uesato et al., 2022; Lightman et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024b; Setlur et al., 2024) effectively imposes all-step-correct (product) aggregations over per-step verifiers, matching the all-success example for which we establish an exponential Ω⁡(2H)\Omega(2^{H}) lower bound. RLHF with KL regularization (Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023; Xiong et al., 2024) replaces the standard additive return with a non-cumulative criterion closely related to the exponential-utility / entropic-risk instance covered in Appendix H. Compared with these lines, we develop the first finite-sample-complexity theory for offline RL under generalized trajectory-level objectives, and characterize tractable regimes through the reward-process coefficient κμ​(σ)\kappa_{\mu}(\sigma) and the Bellman inverse coefficient χμ​(σ)\chi_{\mu}(\sigma).

Appendix B Technical Lemmas for Outcome-based Offline RL

This appendix uses the following population loss notation throughout. For a policy π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, a candidate reward r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}, and a critic f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, define

ℒμ​(π,f)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mu}(\pi,f) ≔∑h=1H𝔼μ​[fh​(sh,π)−fh​(sh,ah)],\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[f_{h}(s_{h},\pi)-f_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})\right], (18a)
ℒμBE​(π,r,f)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{BE}}(\pi,r,f) ≔∑h=1H𝔼μ​[((f−𝒯rπ​f)​(sh,ah))2],\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[\left((f-{\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f)(s_{h},a_{h})\right)^{2}\right], (18b)
ℒμRM​(r)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r) ≔𝔼μ​[(∑h=1H(rh−rh⋆)​(sh,ah))2]=𝔼μ​[(R⁡(τ,r)−R⋆​(τ))2].\displaystyle\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[\left(\sum_{h=1}^{H}(r_{h}-r_{h}^{\star})(s_{h},a_{h})\right)^{2}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[(R(\tau;r)-R^{\star}(\tau))^{2}\right]. (18c)

B.1 Change-of-Measure and Optimization Tools

This subsection collects the two auxiliary tools used to control the change-of-measure terms and the policy-optimization term in the proof of the upper bound.

The following statement follows from Lemma 1 or Corollary 6 of Yuan et al. (2025).

Lemma 7 (Change of trajectory measure).

For any finite-horizon MDP, behaviour policy μ\mu, target policy π\pi, and bounded measurable function g:𝒮×𝒜→ℝg:{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R} with 𝔼μ​[(∑h=1Hg⁡(sh,ah))2]>0\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[(\sum_{h=1}^{H}g(s_{h},a_{h}))^{2}]>0, we have

(𝔼π​[∑h=1Hg⁡(sh,ah)])2𝔼μ​[(∑h=1Hg⁡(sh,ah))2]≤H​Cs​a​(π).\displaystyle\frac{\left(\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{h=1}^{H}g(s_{h},a_{h})\right]\right)^{2}}{\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[\left(\sum_{h=1}^{H}g(s_{h},a_{h})\right)^{2}\right]}\leq HC_{sa}(\pi).

The next lemma is the standard exponential-weights no-regret bound (Freund and Schapire, 1997; Cesa-Bianchi and Lugosi, 2006), specialised to our layer-wise policy update; we include the proof for completeness.

Lemma 8 (No-regret bound).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a finite action space with |𝒜|<∞|\mathcal{A}|<\infty, and let

Π={π=(π1,…,πH):πh:𝒮h→Δ(𝒜),h∈[H]}\displaystyle\Pi=\bigl\{\pi=(\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{H}):\pi_{h}:{\mathcal{S}}_{h}\to\Delta(\mathcal{A}),\ h\in[H]\bigr\}

be the class of non-stationary policies. Let {fk}k=1K⊂ℱ\{f_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}\subset\mathcal{F} be an arbitrary (possibly data-adaptive) sequence of critics such that, for every k∈[K]k\in[K] and h∈[H]h\in[H],

fk,h:𝒮h×𝒜→[0,Vmax].\displaystyle f_{k,h}:{\mathcal{S}}_{h}\times\mathcal{A}\to[0,V_{\max}].

Set η=Vmax​K/(8​log⁡|𝒜|)\eta=V_{\max}\sqrt{K/(8\log|\mathcal{A}|)} in the update below. Initialize

π1,h(⋅∣s)=Unif(𝒜),∀h∈[H],s∈𝒮h,\displaystyle\pi_{1,h}(\cdot\mid s)=\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{A}),\qquad\forall h\in[H],\ s\in{\mathcal{S}}_{h},

and for each k=1,…,K−1k=1,\dots,K-1 and h∈[H]h\in[H], update

πk+1,h​(a∣s)=πk,h​(a∣s)​exp⁡(fk,h​(s,a)/η)∑a′∈𝒜πk,h​(a′∣s)​exp⁡(fk,h​(s,a′)/η).\displaystyle\pi_{k+1,h}(a\mid s)=\frac{\pi_{k,h}(a\mid s)\exp\bigl(f_{k,h}(s,a)/\eta\bigr)}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\pi_{k,h}(a^{\prime}\mid s)\exp\bigl(f_{k,h}(s,a^{\prime})/\eta\bigr)}. (19)

For any comparator π∈Π\pi\in\Pi, let dh,Sπ​(s)≔∑a∈𝒜hdhπ​(s,a)d_{h,S}^{\pi}(s)\coloneqq\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{h}}d_{h}^{\pi}(s,a) denote the step-hh state marginal, and define

Regk(π)≔∑h=1H𝔼s∼dh,Sπ[𝔼a∼πh(⋅∣s)[fk,h(s,a)]−𝔼a∼πk,h(⋅∣s)[fk,h(s,a)]].\displaystyle\mathrm{Reg}_{k}(\pi)\coloneqq\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{h,S}^{\pi}}\Bigl[\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{h}(\cdot\mid s)}[f_{k,h}(s,a)]-\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{k,h}(\cdot\mid s)}[f_{k,h}(s,a)]\Bigr].

Then, for every comparator π∈Π\pi\in\Pi,

1K​∑k=1KRegk​(π)≤H​Vmax​log⁡|𝒜|2​K.\displaystyle\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{Reg}_{k}(\pi)\leq HV_{\max}\sqrt{\frac{\log|\mathcal{A}|}{2K}}. (20)
Proof.

We prove a pointwise regret bound for each fixed pair (s,h)(s,h), and then average over s∼dh,Sπs\sim d_{h,S}^{\pi} and sum over hh.

Fix any h∈[H]h\in[H] and s∈𝒮hs\in{\mathcal{S}}_{h}. Define

qk(⋅)≔πk,h(⋅∣s),gk(⋅)≔fk,h(s,⋅)∈[0,Vmax]|𝒜|.\displaystyle q_{k}(\cdot)\coloneqq\pi_{k,h}(\cdot\mid s),\qquad g_{k}(\cdot)\coloneqq f_{k,h}(s,\cdot)\in[0,V_{\max}]^{|\mathcal{A}|}.

Then Eq. 19 becomes the exponential-weights update

qk+1​(a)=qk​(a)​exp⁡(gk​(a)/η)∑a′∈𝒜qk​(a′)​exp⁡(gk​(a′)/η).\displaystyle q_{k+1}(a)=\frac{q_{k}(a)\exp(g_{k}(a)/\eta)}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}q_{k}(a^{\prime})\exp(g_{k}(a^{\prime})/\eta)}.

Introduce weights

w1​(a)=q1​(a)=1|𝒜|,wk+1​(a)=wk​(a)​exp⁡(gk​(a)/η),\displaystyle w_{1}(a)=q_{1}(a)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|},\qquad w_{k+1}(a)=w_{k}(a)\exp(g_{k}(a)/\eta),

and let Wk≔∑a∈𝒜wk​(a)W_{k}\coloneqq\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}w_{k}(a). Since W1=1W_{1}=1 and qk​(a)=wk​(a)/Wkq_{k}(a)=w_{k}(a)/W_{k},

Wk+1Wk=∑a∈𝒜qk​(a)​exp⁡(gk​(a)/η)=𝔼a∼qk​[exp⁡(gk​(a)/η)].\displaystyle\frac{W_{k+1}}{W_{k}}=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}q_{k}(a)\exp(g_{k}(a)/\eta)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q_{k}}\bigl[\exp(g_{k}(a)/\eta)\bigr].

Upper bound on log⁡WK+1\log W_{K+1}

By Hoeffding’s lemma, since gk​(a)/η∈[0,Vmax/η]g_{k}(a)/\eta\in[0,V_{\max}/\eta] for all a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A},

log⁡𝔼a∼qk​[exp⁡(gk​(a)/η)]≤1η​𝔼a∼qk​[gk​(a)]+Vmax28​η2.\displaystyle\log\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q_{k}}\bigl[\exp(g_{k}(a)/\eta)\bigr]\leq\frac{1}{\eta}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q_{k}}[g_{k}(a)]+\frac{V_{\max}^{2}}{8\eta^{2}}.

Summing over k=1,…,Kk=1,\dots,K and using W1=1W_{1}=1,

log⁡WK+1≤1η​∑k=1K𝔼a∼qk​[gk​(a)]+Vmax2​K8​η2.\displaystyle\log W_{K+1}\leq\frac{1}{\eta}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q_{k}}[g_{k}(a)]+\frac{V_{\max}^{2}K}{8\eta^{2}}. (21)

Lower bound on log⁡WK+1\log W_{K+1}

WK+1=∑a∈𝒜q1​(a)​exp⁡(1η​∑k=1Kgk​(a)).\displaystyle W_{K+1}=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}q_{1}(a)\exp\left(\frac{1}{\eta}\sum_{k=1}^{K}g_{k}(a)\right).

Since q1=Unif⁡(𝒜)q_{1}=\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{A}) is strictly positive, we can write, for any p∈Δ⁡(𝒜)p\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}),

WK+1=∑a∈𝒜p⁡(a)⋅q1​(a)p⁡(a)​exp⁡(1η​∑k=1Kgk​(a))=𝔼a∼p​[q1​(a)p⁡(a)​exp⁡(1η​∑k=1Kgk​(a))].\displaystyle W_{K+1}=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}p(a)\cdot\frac{q_{1}(a)}{p(a)}\exp\left(\frac{1}{\eta}\sum_{k=1}^{K}g_{k}(a)\right)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}\left[\frac{q_{1}(a)}{p(a)}\exp\left(\frac{1}{\eta}\sum_{k=1}^{K}g_{k}(a)\right)\right].

Applying Jensen’s inequality to the concave function log⁡(⋅)\log(\cdot) yields

logWK+1≥𝔼a∼p[logq1​(a)p⁡(a)+1η∑k=1Kgk(a)]=1η∑k=1K𝔼a∼p[gk(a)]−KL(p∥q1).\displaystyle\log W_{K+1}\geq\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}\left[\log\frac{q_{1}(a)}{p(a)}+\frac{1}{\eta}\sum_{k=1}^{K}g_{k}(a)\right]=\frac{1}{\eta}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}[g_{k}(a)]-\mathrm{KL}(p\|q_{1}).

Combining with Eq. 21 gives

∑k=1K(𝔼a∼p[gk(a)]−𝔼a∼qk[gk(a)])≤ηKL(p∥q1)+Vmax2​K8​η.\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}[g_{k}(a)]-\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q_{k}}[g_{k}(a)]\bigr)\leq\eta\mathrm{KL}(p\|q_{1})+\frac{V_{\max}^{2}K}{8\eta}.

Since q1=Unif⁡(𝒜)q_{1}=\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{A}),

KL(p∥q1)=∑a∈𝒜p(a)log(p(a)|𝒜|)=log|𝒜|+∑a∈𝒜p(a)logp(a)≤log|𝒜|,\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}(p\|q_{1})=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}p(a)\log\bigl(p(a)|\mathcal{A}|\bigr)=\log|\mathcal{A}|+\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}p(a)\log p(a)\leq\log|\mathcal{A}|,

where the last inequality uses ∑ap⁡(a)​log⁡p⁡(a)≤0\sum_{a}p(a)\log p(a)\leq 0 for any probability distribution pp. Hence, for every p∈Δ⁡(𝒜)p\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}),

∑k=1K(𝔼a∼p​[gk​(a)]−𝔼a∼qk​[gk​(a)])≤η​log⁡|𝒜|+Vmax2​K8​η.\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}[g_{k}(a)]-\mathbb{E}_{a\sim q_{k}}[g_{k}(a)]\bigr)\leq\eta\log|\mathcal{A}|+\frac{V_{\max}^{2}K}{8\eta}. (22)

Setting p(⋅)=πh(⋅∣s)p(\cdot)=\pi_{h}(\cdot\mid s), recalling gk​(a)=fk,h​(s,a)g_{k}(a)=f_{k,h}(s,a) and qk(⋅)=πk,h(⋅∣s)q_{k}(\cdot)=\pi_{k,h}(\cdot\mid s), Eq. 22 becomes a deterministic (pointwise-in-ss) inequality. Taking 𝔼s∼dh,Sπ​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{h,S}^{\pi}}[\cdot] preserves it, and summing over h=1,…,Hh=1,\dots,H yields the intermediate bound

∑k=1KRegk​(π)≤H⁡(η​log⁡|𝒜|+Vmax2​K8​η).\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{Reg}_{k}(\pi)\leq H\left(\eta\log|\mathcal{A}|+\frac{V_{\max}^{2}K}{8\eta}\right). (23)

Finally, when |𝒜|≥2|\mathcal{A}|\geq 2, AM–GM minimizes the right-hand side of Eq. 23 over η>0\eta>0 at

η⋆=Vmax​K8​log⁡|𝒜|,η⋆​log⁡|𝒜|+Vmax2​K8​η⋆=Vmax​K​log⁡|𝒜|2,\displaystyle\eta^{\star}=V_{\max}\sqrt{\frac{K}{8\log|\mathcal{A}|}},\qquad\eta^{\star}\log|\mathcal{A}|+\frac{V_{\max}^{2}K}{8\eta^{\star}}=V_{\max}\sqrt{\frac{K\log|\mathcal{A}|}{2}},

and dividing by KK gives Eq. 20. The case |𝒜|=1|\mathcal{A}|=1 is trivial. ∎

B.2 Concentration Lemmas

This subsection collects the high-probability estimates used to transfer the population losses in the analysis to their empirical counterparts.

Lemma 9 (Uniform concentration of the policy loss).

Assume every f=(f1,…,fH)∈ℱf=(f_{1},\dots,f_{H})\in\mathcal{F} satisfies fh​(s,a)∈[0,Vmax]f_{h}(s,a)\in[0,V_{\max}] for all h∈[H]h\in[H] and (s,a)∈𝒮h×𝒜(s,a)\in{\mathcal{S}}_{h}\times\mathcal{A}, and that 𝒟={τi}i=1n\mathcal{D}=\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} consists of nn i.i.d. trajectories drawn from μ\mu. Fix δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) and define

εPerf≔2​H2​Vmax2​log⁡(2​|Π|​|ℱ|/δ)n.\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Perf}}\coloneqq 2H^{2}V_{\max}^{2}\frac{\log(2|\Pi||\mathcal{F}|/\delta)}{n}. (24)

Then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, simultaneously for every π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and every f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F},

|ℒμ​(π,f)−ℒ𝒟​(π,f)|≤εPerf.\displaystyle\bigl|\mathcal{L}_{\mu}(\pi,f)-\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}(\pi,f)\bigr|\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Perf}}}. (25)
Proof.

Fix (π,f)∈Π×ℱ(\pi,f)\in\Pi\times\mathcal{F}. For each trajectory τi=(si,1,ai,1,…,si,H,ai,H)\tau_{i}=(s_{i,1},a_{i,1},\dots,s_{i,H},a_{i,H}), set

Zi​(π,f)≔∑h=1H[fh​(si,h,π⁡(si,h))−fh​(si,h,ai,h)].\displaystyle Z_{i}(\pi,f)\coloneqq\sum_{h=1}^{H}\bigl[f_{h}(s_{i,h},\pi(s_{i,h}))-f_{h}(s_{i,h},a_{i,h})\bigr].

Since the τi\tau_{i} are i.i.d. under μ\mu, the variables {Zi​(π,f)}i=1n\{Z_{i}(\pi,f)\}_{i=1}^{n} are i.i.d., and by definition of ℒμ​(π,f)\mathcal{L}_{\mu}(\pi,f) and ℒ𝒟​(π,f)\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}(\pi,f) in Section 3,

𝔼τi∼μ​[Zi​(π,f)]=ℒμ​(π,f),1n​∑i=1nZi​(π,f)=ℒ𝒟​(π,f).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{i}\sim\mu}\bigl[Z_{i}(\pi,f)\bigr]=\mathcal{L}_{\mu}(\pi,f),\qquad\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}Z_{i}(\pi,f)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}(\pi,f).

Moreover, since fhf_{h} takes values in [0,Vmax][0,V_{\max}], each summand satisfies

fh​(si,h,π⁡(si,h))−fh​(si,h,ai,h)∈[−Vmax,Vmax],\displaystyle f_{h}(s_{i,h},\pi(s_{i,h}))-f_{h}(s_{i,h},a_{i,h})\in[-V_{\max},V_{\max}],

and therefore |Zi​(π,f)|≤H​Vmax|Z_{i}(\pi,f)|\leq HV_{\max} almost surely. Hoeffding’s inequality applied to the i.i.d. bounded random variables {Zi​(π,f)}i=1n\{Z_{i}(\pi,f)\}_{i=1}^{n} gives, for any δ′∈(0,1)\delta^{\prime}\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ′1-\delta^{\prime},

|ℒμ​(π,f)−ℒ𝒟​(π,f)|≤H​Vmax​2​log⁡(2/δ′)n.\displaystyle\bigl|\mathcal{L}_{\mu}(\pi,f)-\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}(\pi,f)\bigr|\leq HV_{\max}\sqrt{\frac{2\log(2/\delta^{\prime})}{n}}.

Taking a union bound over all pairs (π,f)∈Π×ℱ(\pi,f)\in\Pi\times\mathcal{F} with δ′=δ/(|Π|​|ℱ|)\delta^{\prime}=\delta/(|\Pi||\mathcal{F}|), and noting that H​Vmax​2​log⁡(2​|Π|​|ℱ|/δ)/n=εPerfHV_{\max}\sqrt{2\log(2|\Pi||\mathcal{F}|/\delta)/n}=\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Perf}}} by definition Eq. 24, yields Eq. 25 simultaneously for every (π,f)∈Π×ℱ(\pi,f)\in\Pi\times\mathcal{F}. ∎

Lemma 10 (Reward-model concentration via Bernstein).

Let 𝒟={(τi,Yi)}i=1n\mathcal{D}=\{(\tau_{i},Y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} be nn i.i.d. samples collected under μ\mu, where

Yi=∑h=1Hrh⋆​(si,h,ai,h)+ξi,𝔼⁡[ξi∣τi]=0,|ξi|≤H​ a.s.,\displaystyle Y_{i}=\sum_{h=1}^{H}r^{\star}_{h}(s_{i,h},a_{i,h})+\xi_{i},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\xi_{i}\mid\tau_{i}]=0,\qquad|\xi_{i}|\leq H\text{ a.s.},

Assume r⋆∈ℛr^{\star}\in\mathcal{R} and every r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R} satisfies 0≤rh​(s,a)≤10\leq r_{h}(s,a)\leq 1. Define the population and empirical reward-model losses

ℒμRM​(r)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r) :=𝔼μ​[(∑h=1H(r−r⋆)​(sh,ah))2],\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[\Big(\textstyle\sum_{h=1}^{H}(r-r^{\star})(s_{h},a_{h})\Big)^{2}\right],
ℒ𝒟RM​(r)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r) :=1n​∑i=1n(Yi−∑h=1Hrh​(si,h,ai,h))2.\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(Y_{i}-\textstyle\sum_{h=1}^{H}r_{h}(s_{i,h},a_{i,h})\Big)^{2}.

Then for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, simultaneously for every r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R},

ℒμRM​(r)≤2​[ℒ𝒟RM​(r)−ℒ𝒟RM​(r⋆)]+εRM,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r)\leq 2\bigl[\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r)-\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r^{\star})\bigr]+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{RM}}, (26)

where

εRM=1283⋅H2​log⁡(|ℛ|/δ)n,\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathrm{RM}}=\frac{128}{3}\cdot\frac{H^{2}\log(|\mathcal{R}|/\delta)}{n},
Proof.

Fix any r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R} and write Δi:=∑h=1H(r−r⋆)​(si,h,ai,h)\Delta_{i}:=\sum_{h=1}^{H}(r-r^{\star})(s_{i,h},a_{i,h}). Under the assumption 0≤rh,rh⋆≤10\leq r_{h},r^{\star}_{h}\leq 1 we have |Δi|≤H|\Delta_{i}|\leq H. A direct expansion gives

(Yi−∑hr)2−(Yi−∑hr⋆)2=(Δi−ξi)2−ξi2=Δi2−2​Δi​ξi,\displaystyle\bigl(Y_{i}-\textstyle\sum_{h}r\bigr)^{2}-\bigl(Y_{i}-\sum_{h}r^{\star}\bigr)^{2}=(\Delta_{i}-\xi_{i})^{2}-\xi_{i}^{2}=\Delta_{i}^{2}-2\Delta_{i}\xi_{i},

so, letting Ui​(r):=Δi2−2​Δi​ξiU_{i}(r):=\Delta_{i}^{2}-2\Delta_{i}\xi_{i},

ℒ𝒟RM​(r)−ℒ𝒟RM​(r⋆)=1n​∑i=1nUi​(r).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r)-\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r^{\star})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}U_{i}(r). (27)

Mean. Since 𝔼⁡[ξi∣τi]=0\mathbb{E}[\xi_{i}\mid\tau_{i}]=0,

𝔼⁡[Ui​(r)]=𝔼⁡[Δi2]−2​𝔼​[Δi​𝔼​[ξi∣τi]]=𝔼⁡[Δi2]=ℒμRM​(r).\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[U_{i}(r)]=\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{i}^{2}]-2\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{i}\mathbb{E}[\xi_{i}\mid\tau_{i}]]=\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{i}^{2}]=\mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r). (28)

Var⁡(Ui​(r))=Var⁡(Δi2)+4​V​a​r​(Δi​ξi).\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(U_{i}(r))=\mathrm{Var}(\Delta_{i}^{2})+4\mathrm{Var}(\Delta_{i}\xi_{i}).

Each term is self-bounded by ℒμRM​(r)\mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r):

Var⁡(Δi2)≤𝔼⁡[Δi4]≤H2​𝔼​[Δi2]=H2​ℒμRM​(r),\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(\Delta_{i}^{2})\leq\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{i}^{4}]\leq H^{2}\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{i}^{2}]=H^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r),

Var⁡(Δi​ξi)=𝔼⁡[Δi2​ξi2]=𝔼⁡[Δi2​𝔼​[ξi2∣τi]]≤H2​ℒμRM​(r).\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(\Delta_{i}\xi_{i})=\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{i}^{2}\xi_{i}^{2}]=\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{i}^{2}\mathbb{E}[\xi_{i}^{2}\mid\tau_{i}]]\leq H^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r).

Combining,

Var⁡(Ui​(r))≤5​H2​ℒμRM​(r).\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(U_{i}(r))\leq 5H^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r). (29)

Range. Since |ξi|≤H|\xi_{i}|\leq H, |Ui​(r)|≤H2+2​H2=3​H2|U_{i}(r)|\leq H^{2}+2H^{2}=3H^{2}. We use the looser bound |Ui​(r)|≤M:=8​H2|U_{i}(r)|\leq M:=8H^{2}, so that |Ui​(r)−𝔼​Ui​(r)|≤2​M|U_{i}(r)-\mathbb{E}U_{i}(r)|\leq 2M.

Bernstein and self-bounding. Apply one-sided Bernstein to the i.i.d. variables {Ui​(r)}i=1n\{U_{i}(r)\}_{i=1}^{n} with confidence η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1), using Eq. 28–Eq. 29 and the centered range bound 2​M2M: with probability at least 1−η1-\eta,

ℒμRM​(r)−[ℒ𝒟RM​(r)−ℒ𝒟RM​(r⋆)]≤10​H2​ℒμRM​(r)​log⁡(1/η)n+2​M​log⁡(1/η)3​n.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r)-\bigl[\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r)-\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r^{\star})\bigr]\leq\sqrt{\frac{10H^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r)\log(1/\eta)}{n}}+\frac{2M\log(1/\eta)}{3n}.

Taking η=δ/|ℛ|\eta=\delta/|\mathcal{R}| and a union bound over r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}, set

x:=ℒμRM​(r),T:=ℒ𝒟RM​(r)−ℒ𝒟RM​(r⋆),β′:=4​H2​log⁡(|ℛ|/δ)n.x:=\mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r),\qquad T:=\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r)-\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{RM}}(r^{\star}),\qquad\beta^{\prime}:=4H^{2}\frac{\log(|\mathcal{R}|/\delta)}{n}.

x≤T+8​β′​x+43​β′.\displaystyle x\leq T+\sqrt{8\beta^{\prime}x}+\frac{4}{3}\beta^{\prime}. (30)

Finally, 8​β′​x≤x/2+4​β′\sqrt{8\beta^{\prime}x}\leq x/2+4\beta^{\prime} by AM-GM. Substituting this into Eq. 30 and moving x/2x/2 to the left gives

x≤2​T+323​β′=2​T+1283⋅H2​log⁡(|ℛ|/δ)n,x\leq 2T+\frac{32}{3}\beta^{\prime}=2T+\frac{128}{3}\cdot\frac{H^{2}\log(|\mathcal{R}|/\delta)}{n},

which is Eq. 26. ∎

For a critic ff and policy π\pi, write Vf,hπ​(s):=fh​(s,πh)V_{f,h}^{\pi}(s):=f_{h}(s,\pi_{h}) and set Vf,H+1π≡0V_{f,H+1}^{\pi}\equiv 0. In the outcome-based setting, the Bellman error in Eq. 3b is computed by plugging in the candidate reward rr; no observed per-step reward is used.

Lemma 11 (Bellman-error concentration).

Assume Π,ℛ,ℱ\Pi,\mathcal{R},\mathcal{F} are finite, every r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R} satisfies 0≤rh​(s,a)≤10\leq r_{h}(s,a)\leq 1, every f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} satisfies 0≤fh​(s,a)≤H0\leq f_{h}(s,a)\leq H, and uniform approximate Bellman completeness holds with error εℱ,ℱ\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}} (Assumption 3). Then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the following holds simultaneously for all (π,r,f)∈Π×ℛ×ℱ(\pi,r,f)\in\Pi\times\mathcal{R}\times\mathcal{F}:

ℒμBE​(π,r,f)≤2​ℒ𝒟BE​(π,r,f)+εBE+4​εℱ,ℱ,εBE≔2563⋅H3​log⁡(2​|Π​‖ℛ‖​ℱ|/δ)n.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{BE}}(\pi,r,f)\leq 2\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{D}}^{\mathrm{BE}}(\pi,r,f)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{BE}}+4\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}},\qquad\varepsilon_{\mathrm{BE}}\coloneqq\frac{256}{3}\cdot\frac{H^{3}\log\bigl(2|\Pi||\mathcal{R}||\mathcal{F}|/\delta\bigr)}{n}.
Proof.

Fix any (π,r,f)∈Π×ℛ×ℱ(\pi,r,f)\in\Pi\times\mathcal{R}\times\mathcal{F}. For any bounded gg, define the population and empirical unminimized Bellman-regression residuals

Lμ​(g)\displaystyle L_{\mu}(g) :=∑h=1H𝔼μ​[(gh​(sh,ah)−rh​(sh,ah)−fh+1​(sh+1,π))2],\displaystyle:=\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{\mu}\left[\bigl(g_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})-r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})-f_{h+1}(s_{h+1},\pi)\bigr)^{2}\right],
L𝒟​(g)\displaystyle L_{\mathcal{D}}(g) :=1n​∑i=1n∑h=1H(gh​(si,h,ai,h)−rh​(si,h,ai,h)−fh+1​(si,h+1,π))2.\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\bigl(g_{h}(s_{i,h},a_{i,h})-r_{h}(s_{i,h},a_{i,h})-f_{h+1}(s_{i,h+1},\pi)\bigr)^{2}.

The key observation is that rh​(sh,ah)r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h}) is deterministic given (sh,ah)(s_{h},a_{h}), so conditioning on (sh,ah)(s_{h},a_{h}),

𝔼[rh(sh,ah)+Vf,h+1π(sh+1)|sh,ah]=rh(sh,ah)+𝔼[Vf,h+1π(sh+1)∣sh,ah]=(𝒯rπf)h(sh,ah),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})+V_{f,h+1}^{\pi}(s_{h+1})\middle|s_{h},a_{h}\right]=r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})+\mathbb{E}[V_{f,h+1}^{\pi}(s_{h+1})\mid s_{h},a_{h}]=({\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f)_{h}(s_{h},a_{h}),

and moreover Var⁡(rh​(sh,ah)+Vf,h+1π​(sh+1)∣sh,ah)=Var⁡(Vf,h+1π​(sh+1)∣sh,ah)\mathrm{Var}(r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})+V_{f,h+1}^{\pi}(s_{h+1})\mid s_{h},a_{h})=\mathrm{Var}(V_{f,h+1}^{\pi}(s_{h+1})\mid s_{h},a_{h}), since adding a (sh,ah)(s_{h},a_{h})-measurable constant leaves the conditional variance unchanged. Hence the bias–variance decomposition gives

𝔼[(gh(sh,ah)−rh(sh,ah)−Vf,h+1π(sh+1))2|sh,ah]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\bigl(g_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})-r_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})-V_{f,h+1}^{\pi}(s_{h+1})\bigr)^{2}\middle|s_{h},a_{h}\right]
=(gh(sh,ah)−(𝒯rπf)h(sh,ah))2+Var(Vf,h+1π(sh+1)|sh,ah).\displaystyle\qquad=\bigl(g_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})-({\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f)_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})\bigr)^{2}+\mathrm{Var}\left(V_{f,h+1}^{\pi}(s_{h+1})\middle|s_{h},a_{h}\right).

Taking expectation over (sh,ah)∼dhμ(s_{h},a_{h})\sim d_{h}^{\mu} and summing over h=1,…,Hh=1,\dots,H, we obtain

Lμ(g)=∥g−𝒯rπf∥2,μ2+∑h=1H𝔼dhμ[Var(Vf,h+1π(sh+1)|sh,ah)].\displaystyle L_{\mu}(g)=\|g-{\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f\|_{2,\mu}^{2}+\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{d_{h}^{\mu}}\left[\mathrm{Var}\left(V_{f,h+1}^{\pi}(s_{h+1})\middle|s_{h},a_{h}\right)\right]. (31)

The second term does not depend on gg. Hence, setting g=fg=f and g=𝒯rπ​fg={\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f in Eq. 31, we obtain

Lμ​(f)−Lμ​(𝒯rπ​f)=‖f−𝒯rπ​f‖2,μ2=ℒμBE​(π,r,f),\displaystyle L_{\mu}(f)-L_{\mu}({\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f)=\|f-{\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f\|_{2,\mu}^{2}=\mathcal{L}_{\mu}^{\mathrm{BE}}(\pi,r,f), (32)

For each trajectory ii, define

Zi​(π,r,f)\displaystyle Z_{i}(\pi,r,f) :=∑h=1H[ℓi,h​(f,π,r,f)−ℓi,h​(𝒯rπ​f,π,r,f)],\displaystyle:=\sum_{h=1}^{H}\Bigl[\ell_{i,h}(f;\pi,r,f)-\ell_{i,h}({\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f;\pi,r,f)\Bigr],

ℓi,h​(g,π,r,f):=(gh​(si,h,ai,h)−rh​(si,h,ai,h)−Vf,h+1π​(si,h+1))2.\displaystyle\ell_{i,h}(g;\pi,r,f):=\bigl(g_{h}(s_{i,h},a_{i,h})-r_{h}(s_{i,h},a_{i,h})-V_{f,h+1}^{\pi}(s_{i,h+1})\bigr)^{2}.

Since the trajectories are i.i.d., the variables {Zi​(π,r,f)}i=1n\{Z_{i}(\pi,r,f)\}_{i=1}^{n} are i.i.d. Moreover, by Eq. 32,

Therefore

≤4​H​|Ai,h−Bi,h|.\displaystyle\leq 4H|A_{i,h}-B_{i,h}|.

(Ai,h2−Bi,h2)2≤16​H2​(fh​(si,h,ai,h)−(𝒯rπ​f)h​(si,h,ai,h))2.\displaystyle\bigl(A_{i,h}^{2}-B_{i,h}^{2}\bigr)^{2}\leq 16H^{2}\bigl(f_{h}(s_{i,h},a_{i,h})-({\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f)_{h}(s_{i,h},a_{i,h})\bigr)^{2}. (34)

Zi​(π,r,f)2\displaystyle Z_{i}(\pi,r,f)^{2} =(∑h=1H[ℓi,h​(f,π,r,f)−ℓi,h​(𝒯rπ​f,π,r,f)])2\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{h=1}^{H}\bigl[\ell_{i,h}(f;\pi,r,f)-\ell_{i,h}({\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f;\pi,r,f)\bigr]\right)^{2}
≤H​∑h=1H[ℓi,h​(f,π,r,f)−ℓi,h​(𝒯rπ​f,π,r,f)]2\displaystyle\leq H\sum_{h=1}^{H}\bigl[\ell_{i,h}(f;\pi,r,f)-\ell_{i,h}({\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f;\pi,r,f)\bigr]^{2}
≤16​H3​∑h=1H(fh​(si,h,ai,h)−(𝒯rπ​f)h​(si,h,ai,h))2,\displaystyle\leq 16H^{3}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\bigl(f_{h}(s_{i,h},a_{i,h})-({\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f)_{h}(s_{i,h},a_{i,h})\bigr)^{2},

≤16​H3​∑h=1H𝔼dhμ​[(fh​(sh,ah)−(𝒯rπ​f)h​(sh,ah))2]\displaystyle\leq 16H^{3}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{d_{h}^{\mu}}\left[\bigl(f_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})-({\mathcal{T}}_{r}^{\pi}f)_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})\bigr)^{2}\right]

T⁡(π,r,f)≤εℱ,ℱ+8​β​εℱ,ℱ+43​β≤2​εℱ,ℱ+163​β,\displaystyle T(\pi,r,f)\leq\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}}+\sqrt{8\beta\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}}}+\frac{4}{3}\beta\leq 2\varepsilon_{\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F}}+\frac{16}{3}\beta, (41)
